title: Jalte lakdi mein saanp bacha kar Parshvanath ne kya paaya?
hooks: Ek jalta lakdi... andar saanp phansa tha
Rajkumar Parshvanath ne saanp ko bachaya... kaise?
Ek saanp ka badla... do janam tak kaise chala?
hook_why: Opens with immediate visual danger (burning log + trapped snake) in the first spoken words, satisfying the sound-off visual loop requirement — fire and snake are visible before any voice registers; named entity Parshvanath arrives in the very next line.
metaphor: Burning log as karmic mirror — the fire reveals the hidden past-life debt and the single act of compassion that rewrites the future.
mechanism: Prince Parshvanath hears a snake crying inside a burning log during sage Katha's panchatapa
He reaches into the fire and pulls the snake out, choosing compassion over safety
The snake is Kamath, his past-life enemy who killed him as Marubhuti and again in later births
Compassion breaks the karmic revenge cycle; the snake dies and is reborn as Dharanendra and Padmavati
Later, during Parshvanath's meditation, Dharanendra and Padmavati shield him from Meghmali's storm with a serpent canopy
That canopy becomes Parshvanath's eternal iconographic emblem — the snake hood over the Tirthankara

cast.Prince Parshvanath: young prince in ancient Indian royal attire — silk dhoti, jeweled necklace, calm compassionate face, dark hair tied in a topknot, standing barefoot on marble
cast.Sage Katha: elderly Jain ascetic in plain white unstitched cotton robes, carrying a soft white whisk broom (rajoharan), seated in meditation before a fire altar
cast.Snake pair: two divine serpents with multi-hooded crowns, iridescent scales, golden eyes, coiled together — one male (Dharanendra), one female (Padmavati), radiating gentle light
cast.Demon Meghmali: dark storm-cloud figure with fierce eyes, riding a black cloud, hurling rain and lightning — never shown attacking the Tirthankara directly

claims.claim: Parshvanatha is the 23rd Tirthankara of Jainism, symbolized by a snake canopy.
claims.basis: Wikipedia: Pārśvanātha page lists symbol as Snake, predecessor Neminatha, successor Mahavira.

claims.claim: Prince Parshvanatha saved a snake trapped in a burning log during sage Katha's panchatapa austerity.
claims.basis: Hindu-blog.com article on Parshvanatha sculpture symbolism cites Kalpa-sutra: 'Parshvanatha once saved a serpent that had been trapped in a log in an ascetic's fire.'

claims.claim: The snake was Kamath, Parshvanatha's past-life enemy who killed him as Marubhuti and in subsequent births.
claims.basis: Jainworld.com 'Parshvanath Bhagavan – 23' details past incarnations: Marubhuti killed by brother Kamath; Kamath reborn as serpent stinging elephant; later as Bhil killing ascetic Vajranabh.

claims.claim: The snake died and was reborn as Dharanendra, who later protected Parshvanatha during meditation from Meghmali's storm along with his consort Padmavati.
claims.basis: Hindu-blog.com: 'The rescued serpent was later reborn as Dharanendra... Padmavati and her husband Dharanendra protected Lord Parshvanatha when he was harassed by Meghmali.'

claims.claim: The serpent canopy (snake hoods) became Parshvanatha's eternal iconographic emblem.
claims.basis: Hindu-blog.com: 'In sculpture and painting he is always identified by a canopy of snake hoods over his head.' Wikipedia confirms symbol is Snake.
